title: 180-Day Closing Coordination
name: 180-Day Closing Coordination
metaDescription: Coordinating a Dallas 1031 exchange from the relinquished-property closing through a funded replacement purchase, all inside one fixed 180-day window.

sections.html: A 1031 exchange gives a Dallas investor exactly 180 days to move from a sold property into a closed replacement, and that clock does not pause for a slow lender, a thin identification list, or a stubborn title curative item. Coordination in this window means keeping every deadline-bound party moving against the same calendar from the first day.

sections.heading: The Countdown Starts at the First Closing, Not the Decision to Exchange
sections.html:
Plenty of investors assume the 180 days begins once they have settled on a strategy or found a replacement they like. It actually starts the day the relinquished property closes and title transfers, whether that property is a warehouse near I-20 or an office suite off the North Dallas Tollway. The 45-day identification window runs concurrently inside that same 180-day period, not before it. Coordination work in the first days focuses on getting the qualified intermediary agreement signed before the relinquished closing funds, since a late-signed exchange agreement can void the exchange outright.

Dallas closings tend to move quickly once a contract is firm, which cuts both ways: it gives the exchange a fast start, but it also means the clock is running before most investors have finished lining up a replacement.

sections.heading: Two Closings, One Deadline, Different Timelines
sections.html: Dallas exchangers are frequently closing a sale in one submarket while trying to lock a purchase in another, moving a Uptown-area asset out while a suburban NNN parcel or a South Dallas industrial building comes in. Those two transactions rarely move at the same pace. A cash buyer can close a relinquished sale in a few weeks while the replacement purchase drags through lender underwriting, survey work, or environmental review. Coordination means building the replacement contract's closing contingencies around the exchange deadline rather than the other way around, so a buyer's financing timeline does not quietly eat into identification days. It also means checking the relinquished sale's own contingencies, inspection periods, financing conditions on the buyer's side, against the same deadline, since a delay on the outgoing sale pushes the entire 180-day clock later along with it.

sections.heading: What Gets Tracked Against the Calendar Every Week
sections.html:
A working exchange calendar for a Dallas transaction typically holds:

  • Relinquished property closing date and funds release to the qualified intermediary
  • 45-day identification deadline and the exact properties named in writing
  • Lender commitment date and appraisal or environmental turnaround
  • Replacement property closing date, set with buffer ahead of day 180
  • Title curative items and survey deadlines on the replacement contract
  • Insurance binder and lender documentation cutoffs

sections.heading: When the Tax Filing Deadline Shortens the Window
sections.html: The 180 days can end earlier than expected if the exchanger's tax return due date, including extensions, falls before day 180 — a detail that trips up first-time exchangers more than any other rule in this process. Filing an extension keeps the full 180 days available and is a routine, unremarkable step, but it has to happen before the original filing deadline. This is a tax filing decision that belongs with the investor's own CPA or tax advisor; the coordination role is flagging the date early enough that the extension actually gets filed, not discovered after the fact.

sections.heading: One Shared Calendar Instead of Five Separate Ones
sections.html: Title companies, lenders, brokers, and qualified intermediaries each run their own internal timelines, and none of them are naturally synced to an exchanger's 180-day limit. The practical fix is a single shared deadline sheet every party works from, updated the moment any date shifts, whether that is a delayed appraisal, a renegotiated closing date, or a lender asking for updated financials. In a market that moves as fast as Dallas commercial real estate, a date slipping by a week on one side of a deal can consume the buffer needed to close the replacement before day 180. The value of a shared calendar is less about any single deadline and more about catching drift early, seeing a lender's commitment letter slip by three days before it compounds into a missed closing window two weeks later.

faqs.q: Does the 180-day period pause if the replacement property closing is delayed by the lender?
faqs.a: No. The 180 days runs on a fixed calendar from the relinquished closing date and does not extend for lender delays, appraisal turnaround, or title issues. Building buffer time into the replacement contract's closing date is the practical way to absorb those delays before they threaten day 180.

faqs.q: Can the 45-day identification period and the 180-day exchange period be extended separately?
faqs.a: Both run from the same start date, the relinquished property's closing, and neither extends on its own outside of a formally declared disaster relief period from the IRS. Investors should confirm current disaster relief status with their qualified intermediary or tax advisor if a federally declared disaster affects their transaction.

faqs.q: What happens if my tax return is due before the 180 days are up?
faqs.a: The exchange period ends on whichever comes first, day 180 or the tax return due date for the year of the relinquished sale, including any filed extension. Filing an extension before the original due date preserves the full 180 days, which is why that date needs to be on the calendar from week one.

faqs.q: How early should the replacement property closing be scheduled relative to day 180?
faqs.a: Most coordination plans target a closing at least one to two weeks ahead of the actual deadline, leaving room for last-minute lender conditions, title curative items, or wire timing issues that come up in Dallas's fast-moving closing schedules.

faqs.q: Who holds the exchange proceeds during this period?
faqs.a: A qualified intermediary holds the funds from the relinquished sale in escrow for the full exchange period. The exchanger never takes actual or constructive receipt of the funds, which is one of the requirements that keeps the exchange valid.
